data: Cape Canaveral Mercury-Atlas pad — launched all 4 orbital Mercury flights (Glenn / Carpenter / Schirra / Cooper, 1962-1963)

Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 14 hosted Atlas missile tests then the four orbital Mercury-Atlas crewed missions: Friendship 7 (1962-02-20, Glenn — first American in orbit), Aurora 7 (1962-05-24, Carpenter), Sigma 7 (1962-10-03, Schirra), and Faith 7 (1963-05-15, Cooper). After Mercury, LC-14 hosted four Atlas-Agena uncrewed missions before being deactivated in 1967. A steel Mercury 7 monument was dedicated on November 10, 1964 at the pad. The launch ring + service tower base remain visible.

If Complex 5 is where Americans first touched space, Complex 14 is where they first stayed. This was the Atlas pad, and all four orbital Mercury flights left from it — Glenn, Carpenter, Schirra, Cooper — the flights that put an American in orbit rather than on an arc. It later launched the Gemini-Atlas target vehicles that taught crews to rendezvous, so the same patch of ground bridges the first orbits and the docking skills Apollo would need. Where 5 holds the starting line, 14 holds the moment the United States became a genuinely orbital nation.
First American to orbit the Earth
Repeated Glenn's 3-orbit profile; overshot landing target by 400 km
First textbook Mercury flight — 6 orbits; double Glenn / Carpenter duration
Last solo American orbital flight; 22 orbits / 34 hours
Cape Canaveral Mercury-Redstone pad — launched Freedom 7 (Shepard, 1961-05-05) and Liberty Bell 7 (Grissom, 1961-07-21)
Thor and Delta pad pair: Spirit, Opportunity, Pathfinder, MESSENGER, Dawn; demolished in 2018
Sputnik 1 (1957). Vostok 1 — Gagarin (1961). Five hundred and forty Soyuz launches from a single pad.
Active Soyuz crewed pad — every ISS Soyuz crew rotation since 2020 has lifted from Site 31
NASA pad at Cape Canaveral (1961-68) — first Saturn I; Apollo 1 fire site 1967-01-27; Apollo 7 first crewed launch 1968-10-11
Polar / sun-synchronous gateway — Falcon 9 to Starlink + national-security + earth-observation
